Description:
The OA only had multiple choice questions. There were timed sections and no negative marking. The different sections were mainly probability and statistics, finance, Python and OOPS and AI/ML. There were no coding questions to my surprise. Also, some of these questions were repeated from the BIIC Mentorship test which was held a few months back. You need to keep track of time, don’t spend too much time on a single question, and focus first on the ones you’re confident about in that section. Since, there's no negative marking, attempt all of them. I was aiming for the AI/ML role only. For this, Nipun Sir’s Slides from the Introduction to ML course is helpful. Some external resources which are helpful for the OA (and more helpful for the interviews to revise a day before) are:
1] top 50 ml interview questions on gfg
2] top data science questions on gfg
3] 30 OOPs Interview Questions and Answers
4] Python Interview Questions and Answers
Interview Round 1:
Platform: Offline/In-person
Duration: ~45 minutes
The interview started with my introduction. Then we discussed the projects on my resume in detail. This was followed by a mix of technical and behavioral questions, for which I hadn’t done any specific preparation. For each of them, I took instances from my resume to answer them. Some of them which I remember are - where have you used ai for automation, was there a time where you made a major mistake and how did you handle it, have you lead a team, what are the major challenges you have faced working on a project involving ai, have you handled the logistics and costs involving ai projects,etc. They weren’t exactly the same, but they were of similar kind.
Following this, the interviewer asked more technical questions. We started with the basics of ML. Questions were majorly on decision trees, bias and variance, data imbalance, boosting techniques, regularization (L1 and L2), activation functions, gradient descent and MLP’s. All the questions focused on testing your fundamentals, which should be straightforward if you've followed the ML course diligently (for example - what is the advantage of L1 regularization over L2 regularization and why, how do you compute the differential of regularization term in L1 regularization). He also drew certain data distributions (XOR distribution) and asked me to draw decision boundaries for those distributions.
After that, he asked me questions on the basics of python. Topics were lambda functions, list comprehension and some basics of oops. For all these questions, make sure you read the top interview questions for which I have provided the links above. When asked about my interest in finance, I made it clear that my knowledge in finance as of now is limited but I am interested in learning more about it.

SkanAI - Data Scientist Intern.docx:
Test Round: Coding Test
Platform: Glider.AI
Duration: 31 mins(MCQ) + 61 mins(Coding)
Description: 
There were 2 sections. The first section were multiple choice questions (31 minutes) and the second section were DSA problems(61 minutes). Others have given detailed descriptions of these. Refer to those for the questions. Some tips:
1] Revise basic ML(Decision trees, regression, regularization) and DL architectures (RNN, LSTM, GRUs). Use Nipun Sir’s slides from the ML course. You can quickly skim through top 50 ml interview questions on gfg and top data science questions on gfg.
2] Revise basic concepts of probability, statistics (z-test) and dimensionality reduction.
3] For the DSA round, previous year questions were repeated for us. Go through previous year prepmats. Majorly, the topics were graphs, dp and greedy. Try to pass as many test cases as you can. Start with brute force if you are unable to think of any optimized solution. Several test cases usually pass.
Interview Round 1:
Platform: Microsoft Teams 
Duration: 30-45 mins
The interviewers are extremely friendly, so you need not panic. Having good research projects helps immensely. I had worked with Nipun Sir in a semester-long course project and as a SRIP intern. We had submitted a paper to a conference. I had added this to my resume. We spent nearly 25-30 minutes discussing my project, explaining to him my work and results. It was a to and fro conversation. After this, I was asked about decision trees, bias and variance, sampling and boosting techniques. Have complete clarity of these techniques. He also asked me about the dimensionality reduction techniques, mostly PCA (this was also mentioned in my resume as a part of one of my projects) and neural network based dimensionality reduction (Auto encoders). Questions were not broad, they were in-depth (for example, one of the steps in PCA is normalization. Why do we do it? And what happens if we don't do it? What changes will you observe geometrically). Then we concluded with a question for the interviewer. Overall, stay energetic, be clear and think out loud.
Interview Round 2:
Platform: Microsoft Teams
Duration: 45-60 mins
Again, we spent about 20-25 minutes discussing my research project. Then he asked me questions about other projects in my resume. One of them was a multi-agentic RAG project, which I had done as a part of Inter-IIT Tech Meet 13. He asked me to explain the different types of RAG systems (dynamic, corrective, adaptive,...). Another project I had was based on VLM fine-tuning. He asked me about LORA, what is the principle behind it, and how it is implemented (LORA adaptors are inserted between the layers), and QLORA. All in all, you need to be well-versed with every word in your resume. Again questions were not broad, they were in-depth. Clarity of concepts and basics are important.
After this, he asked me a question on attention. I hadn’t done the higher level courses yet (NLP, DL or CV). However, I knew the thought process and intuition. I made this clear to him, and continued to explain the concept, intuition and why it works. Never give up or not answer questions (this doesn’t mean you yap. Approach the problem logically and if you are unable to then don't answer). Think out loud and explain your thought process. Later, he asked me about similarity metrics/ distances (cosine, jaccard, euclidian), and when to use which one. This proceeded to a DSA question. It was the Edit Distance question. Since we were out of time, he explained to me about how they utilized this “edit distance” as a distance metric in one of their ongoing projects. This ended with a question for the interviewer. I further dwelled into their project and asked him follow up questions, suggested him some other strategies, discussing why they would/wouldn’t work. It was a great experience!
Interview Round 3:
Platform: Zoom
Duration: 20-25 mins
This round was different. No introduction, just straight to the point. He started by asking me if I had an idea of what Skan AI does and what expectations I have. Then he proceeded to the questions, which were the same for everybody and are clearly described by them. These questions were completely open-ended and the purpose was to judge the way you think.
For the first question (check the question in others descriptions), it was very simple to come up with the brute force solution (count all different occurring patterns). Always ask back questions for any ambiguity/clarity. This way the interviewer knows you have understood the problem right. Also, dont expect any help from the interviewer in this round😅. I literally ended up explaining 8-9 different methods for that problem (converting into embeddings and then similarity search, Byte Pair encoding, converting into graph nodes and graph search algos,etc..). For every method I would think of, I would reason if it would work or not work. Thinking out loud is the key here. I tried hard to get hints in the end until I had to admit and say “I think I am moving in the wrong direction now, and I don't have more methods left.” The interviewer laughed and then proceeded to the next question.
For the second question, I defined a similarity metric between the boxes based on colors in them. Before I could reach the exact solution, the interviewer was convinced about my thinking direction and the interview ended.

Interview Round 1:
Platform: Microsoft Teams
Duration: ~45 mins
Technical Questions:
The round started with me introducing myself and a brief look through my resume. The interviewer was curious about a ML research project on Graph Neural Networks I had done in my 4th semester as he was exploring that field too and we had a nice brief discussion about the work done. 
The next part of the interview was very unusual. The interviewer opened a HuggingFace ML Challenge which was about designing fusion reactors and asked me to go through it for the next 8 - 10 minutes. He told me to use any AI tools I wanted (infact encouraged me to). After going through it we had a nice discussion on what methodologies could be used to solve the challenge. The interviewer was very friendly and this segment felt more like a conversation.
Then he proceeded to ask me about the main idea behind logistic regression and the loss function that is used and the rationale behind it. He followed up by asking how it could be extended to k-classes instead of 2 classes. 
He then proceeded to ask me a DSA question : Detecting a loop in a linked list. This question is pretty standard and I was able to solve it pretty quickly. And that was about it for the first round. Overall it was pretty laid back and not at all hard difficult wise. 
Interview Round 2:
Platform: Microsoft Teams
Duration: ~45 min
Technical Questions:
This round consisted of  DSA and probability based questions along with ML concepts.
Some of them which I recall were - listing down some activation functions and in what scenarios one would use them (for e.g which activation function could help with vanishing gradients problem) and some others like what PCA is and the need for it. 
I will list all the dsa and probability questions asked below (Courtesy of MS Teams chat history 😉):
Q1:
Given a string s, find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters.
🧪 Example:
vbnetCopyEditInput: s = "abcabcbb" Output: 3 Explanation: The answer is "abc", with the length of 3.
I first explained the brute force approach i.e iterating through every substring and then checking if it has repeating characters and then storing the largest one without repeating characters. 
After this I optimised it by essentially using a sliding window and maintaining a set of characters between the window to bring the time complexity to linear.  
LeetCode : https://leetcode.com/problems/longest-substring-without-repeating-characters/description/
Q2:
Given a 2D grid of '1's (land) and '0's (water), count the number of islands.
An island is surrounded by water and is formed by connecting adjacent lands horizontally or vertically.
🧪 Example:
makefileCopyEditInput:11110
11010
11000
00000
Output: 1
This problem is a very easy application of bfs/dfs. The only thing I would say is to keep your code concise and clean. The solution is pretty simple but you can implement it in a very ugly way.
Q3;
A factory produces electronic chips. Historical data show that 2 % of all chips are faulty.
The quality-control (QC) scanner used to detect faults has the following characteristics:
Sensitivity (true-positive rate) = 95 %
Specificity (true-negative rate) = 90 %
A chip coming off the line is scanned once and the QC machine flags it as “faulty.”
Question: What is the probability that the chip is actually faulty given the flag?
Express your answer as a percentage and show the Bayes-theorem calculation.
I just walked the interviewer through the decision structure and arrived at the final expression using Bayes’ theorem. This was sufficient and I didn't actually need to get a final numerical result.
Q4:
“What is the expected number of fair-coin flips needed to see HT?”
This is a very nice problem. I initially wrote down the first few configurations and was trying to find some pattern but then the interviewer told me to think about the questions in terms of states having some probability of transitioning between each other (Basically Markov Chains).
The following link explains this solution very well : https://math.stackexchange.com/a/947339
Interview Round 3:
Platform: Microsoft Teams
Duration: ~45 mins
Technical Questions:
This round was with the Chief Data Scientist. The main thing to keep in mind is that your assumptions will be challenged and you will be called out for bs. Make sure to keep a very open mind and explore all possibilities while going through the interview. The questions are open ended and are related to problems being solved at the company at the moment so there isn't one right answer. 
Q1:
Given a sequence of activities for a given person throughout the day over a period of time, say 90 days, identify habits i.e common sequence of activities. I spent the first few minutes just asking clarifying questions so I could arrive at the definitive problem statement since the initial question was pretty vague (ig intentionally?).  The logic that I arrived at was that we could do a binary search for the largest length such that a sequence of that length appears every day for that person. To implement the checker function for this binary search we could collect all possible substrings for that length and then use some efficient string matching algo (like string hashing or z function).
Q2:
There is a conveyor belt which has objects of various colors coming in. An object can have any number of colors and the colors the object could be is also not known beforehand. Now we need to classify these objects into some numbers of bins. Once again, I had to ask a lot of clarifying questions and also propose some solutions to arrive at the final problem statement as described above. The final solution I arrived at was - When a new object comes in, calculate a metric of similarity of the object with every bin (Could be done done manually - for eg. average number of colors that match with the incoming object and the other objects in that bin, or some embedding based approach). Now we place the object in the bin which gives the highest similarity score. We also make sure to keep a threshold of score below which the incoming object is placed into an empty bin.
Challenges & Improvements:
Make sure to practice DSA well as it is needed in OA, the level of DSA in interviews is evidently not that high. Make sure to know your projects well and also revise your ML concepts from Nipun Sir’s course well. It is fine to not know Deep Learning topics like Transformers, just convey it to the interviewers and don't try to bs your way to an answer.

Codeforces contests (Not strictly necessary but helps to build aptitude to solve under time pressure)
